      How to answer Gatmaytan’s midterm

      Format, timing, the four question shapes, the ALAC template, and the issue checklist. Read this first, then use it every time you write in the Essay trainer.

      The format you are training for

      • Time: 1 hour 30 minutes for the whole exam (confirmed for this year). With four problems that is about 22 minutes each.
      • Paper: one sheet of yellow paper, front and back, for all answers. Past instructions: if you submit more than one sheet, the sheet with fewer words is the one read.
      • Scoring: each problem is worth 10 points; 70% passes (28 of 40 in 2023).
      • Rules from his past instructions: closed book; identify yourself only by student number; write legibly (“the examiner is not skilled at deciphering hieroglyphics”); “Verbosity is discouraged. This is an examination, not a dissertation.”
      • Grading standard (2015 instructions): “mastery of the subject matter and … ability to present comprehensive and accurate arguments.” The stories “may have been altered”, so read every fact.
      StepMinutesWhat you do
      1. Read and mark3Underline who acted, under what power, the exact words of the law, numbers (votes, days, ages), and dates. Circle the question asked in the last line or the third column.
      2. Spot and outline3Run the checklist below in the margin. Pick the two or three decisive issues. Note one anchor case per issue.
      3. Write14About 150 to 180 words. Answer first, then rule, application, conclusion for each issue.
      4. Check2Did you answer the question actually asked (“resolve in his favor”, “do not raise procedural issues”)? Did you cite the provision and a case?
      Length trap: four answers must share one sheet. Half a page of handwriting per answer is the target. Writing a full page on the first question is the most common way to fail the last one.

      The four question shapes he uses

      1. “Determine the constitutionality of Section X of RA ___” with the text quoted (2023 Q3, 2024 Q2 and Q3). Read every clause; the defect is often in one phrase (an oversight committee’s power to “approve”; a mandate on private parties; an IRR’s publication rule).
      2. “Resolve the legal issues raised by this story” or “critique this official’s statement” (2020 quizzes and finals). You must find every issue, procedural and substantive, and say who is right.
      3. “How does the new law address the issues in [case]?” (2024 Q4, Liban and RA 10530). State the issue the case raised, then show how the statute settles it.
      4. “Assume X challenges this; resolve it in his favor”, sometimes with procedural issues ruled out (2023 Q1, Teves). Argue one side as strongly as the law allows; do not hedge.
      Gatmaytan: His block intel says to start answers with Yes or No, get straight to the case, and use ALAC. He wants your own view of a case and its historical context; where his book criticizes the Court (Javellana, Pangilinan, severability), say so in one line.

      The ALAC template

      A (answer): “Section 4 is unconstitutional.” or “Teves should prevail.”
      L (law): “Under Art. VI, Sec. 16(3), each House may expel a Member with the concurrence of two-thirds of all its Members. In Osmeña v. Pendatun, the Court held …”
      A (application): tie the rule to the exact words of the law or the facts. “Here, Sec. 290-A(4) lets the committee ‘deputize’ the BIR and BOC …”
      C (conclusion): one sentence that answers again. “Hence, the deputization clause is void, but the rest of Sec. 290-A survives under the separability clause.”

      For a two- or three-issue question, repeat L–A–C per issue under short labels (“Procedural:”, “Delegation:”, “Taking:”). Put the strongest counterargument in one sentence only if it is serious, and answer it.

      When to write the procedural layer

      If the question asks you to resolve a case or a petition, start with a two- or three-line procedural paragraph: proper remedy and forum, actual case and ripeness, standing, and any mootness. Skip it when the question says “do not raise procedural issues”, or asks only whether a provision is constitutional (then one line at most).

      Trap: a bill, a draft IRR, or a resolution calling for Charter change is not ripe (Montesclaros; Lozano v. Nograles; In re JDF). If the news is about a proposal, say so first.

      The issue checklist

      Run this in the margin for every problem. The Issue spotter tab drills it.

      1. Court and procedure: actual case; ripeness or mootness (and its four exceptions); standing (citizen, taxpayer, voter, legislator, association or third party, government, environmental); transcendental importance; earliest opportunity; lis mota; proper remedy (Rule 65, declaratory relief) and forum (SC, RTC, COMELEC, HRET or SET, COA).
      2. Who acted and under what power: Congress (plenary but limited), one House, a committee, the President, an agency, an LGU, a private party.
      3. Separation of powers: encroachment; legislative veto or post-enactment role (ABAKADA, Belgica); Congress interpreting the Constitution or overruling the Court (Endencia); adding qualifications to constitutional offices.
      4. Delegation: completeness and sufficient-standard tests; IRR requisites; publication (Tañada) and filing; subdelegation (KMU).
      5. How the law was made: title and one subject; origination of money bills; riders and inappropriate provisions; savings and augmentation; tax exemptions.
      6. Congress internally: officers, quorum, rules, discipline (60-day cap, two-thirds of all members), privileges, incompatible and forbidden offices, tribunals’ jurisdiction, CA composition.
      7. Inherent powers: police power (lawful subject plus lawful means) versus taking (just compensation); non-impairment; state immunity and money claims.
      8. People: natural-born or naturalized; election of citizenship; RA 9225 steps; residence (domicile); suffrage qualifications versus registration rules.

      A model answer at the right length

      2023 Q1 (Teves), in his favor, no procedural issues. About 170 words.

      Answer: The expulsion is void. Although Art. VI, Sec. 16(3) lets the House expel a Member for disorderly behavior by two-thirds of all Members, and no conviction is required (Osmeña v. Pendatun; the power is the House’s own, distinct from criminal liability, cf. De Venecia v. Sandiganbayan), the power must be exercised within the Constitution. First, the grounds are not “disorderly behavior” as a Member: his designation as a terrorist is an executive act, not his conduct in or toward the House, and his absence was already penalized by two 60-day suspensions; expelling him for the same absence punishes him twice and evades the 60-day cap. Second, a dance video and seeking asylum are not acts that obstruct legislative work. Third, the expulsion rests on the killings he has not been tried for (his refusal to join the DOJ probe, the terrorist tag); the House may discipline without a conviction, but it may not turn unproven criminal accusations into the gravest penalty without giving him a real chance to answer them. The expulsion should be set aside.

      Note: This argues one side because the question demands it. In a neutral question, you would add that the Court generally defers to the House on what is disorderly (Osmeña) and that expulsion needs no conviction.

      Interpreting and amending the Constitution

      Syllabus I–II: preliminary readings; principles of interpretation; adoption and amendment (Art. XVII). 17 cases.

      Why the 1987 Constitution reads the way it does

      Gatmaytan’s starting point (book, Chapter 1; ‘Constitutional Amendments as Suspect Projects’): the 1987 Constitution was written after Marcos to place legal obstacles to dictatorship. It expanded judicial review, limited martial law, and made the judiciary independent. It was also a compromise drafted by an elite commission that “hewed closely to the status quo.” Filipinos have never amended it, because every Charter change attempt has been seen as a politician’s project to stay in power.

      Gatmaytan: Charter change proposals are “suspect projects”: they fail unless politicians regain public trust. In an essay on any Charter change story, one line on this context shows mastery.

      The preliminary US readings (Obergefell, 303 Creative, Dobbs) show a court recognizing an unenumerated right, narrowing its effect, and then overruling a precedent by appeal to history and tradition. Use them only as background on how courts change constitutions.

      Principles of interpretation

      PrincipleMeaningCase
      Verba legisWords take their ordinary meaning unless technical terms are used; the Constitution is not a lawyer’s document.J.M. Tuason; Francisco
      Ratio legis est animaWhere the text is unclear, follow the intent of the framers and of the people who ratified it, as shown by the records.Nitafan; Francisco
      Ut magis valeat quam pereatRead the Constitution as a whole; harmonize provisions so every word has effect.Francisco
      Self-executionProvisions are presumed self-executing unless they say legislation is needed; Art. II policies generally are not.Manila Prince Hotel
      ProspectivityConstitutional provisions apply prospectively unless they say otherwise.Filoteo
      Interpretation belongs to courtsCongress cannot declare by statute what a constitutional provision means, still less overrule the Court.Endencia v. David
      Self-executing test (Manila Prince Hotel)
      1. The provision is complete in itself and operative without enabling legislation.
      2. The nature and extent of the right conferred, and the liability imposed, are fixed by the Constitution.
      3. Nothing indicates the subject is referred to Congress for action.
      2026 update (Kapatiran Party v. Congress, decision dated Aug. 26, 2026): the Court held that Art. II, Sec. 26 (‘prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law’) is a mandatory command, abandoned earlier statements that it is not self-executing, and granted mandamus against Congress for 39 years of inaction. Keep three questions apart: (1) Does the provision impose a duty (‘shall’)? (2) Who defines its content (‘as may be defined by law’ means Congress)? (3) Can courts enforce it (grave abuse by inaction under Art. VIII, Sec. 1)? COMELEC still cannot disqualify dynastic candidates without the law. See the case card and the 2026 news watch.

      The judges’ salary line: a lesson in who interprets

      1. Perfecto v. Meer (1950): income tax on a judge’s salary diminished it (1935 Constitution).
      2. Endencia v. David (1953): Congress passed RA 590 declaring such taxation is not a diminution. Void: Congress cannot interpret the Constitution.
      3. Nitafan v. CIR (1987): under the 1987 Constitution the framers intended judges’ salaries to be taxable; Perfecto and Endencia discarded on that point.
      In a news question: when a bill “clarifies” a constitutional term (e.g., defines “natural-born”, “initiate”, or “savings” for constitutional purposes) or responds to a Supreme Court ruling, cite Endencia: Congress makes laws; the Court interprets the Constitution.

      Amendment and revision (Art. XVII)

      Art. XVII, Secs. 1 to 4Section 1. Any amendment to, or revision of, this Constitution may be proposed by: (1) The Congress, upon a vote of three-fourths of all its Members; or (2) A constitutional convention.
      Section 2. Amendments to this Constitution may likewise be directly proposed by the people through initiative upon a petition of at least twelve per centum of the total number of registered voters, of which every legislative district must be represented by at least three per centum of the registered voters therein. No amendment under this section shall be authorized within five years following the ratification of this Constitution nor oftener than once every five years thereafter. The Congress shall provide for the implementation of the exercise of this right.
      Section 3. The Congress may, by a vote of two-thirds of all its Members, call a constitutional convention, or by a majority vote of all its Members, submit to the electorate the question of calling such a convention.
      Section 4. Any amendment to, or revision of, this Constitution under Section 1 hereof shall be valid when ratified by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite which shall be held not earlier than sixty days nor later than ninety days after the approval of such amendment or revision. Any amendment under Section 2 hereof shall be valid when ratified by a majority of the votes cast in a plebiscite which shall be held not earlier than sixty days nor later than ninety days after the certification by the Commission on Elections of the sufficiency of the petition.
      ModeProposalScopeRatification
      Congress as constituent assemblyThree-fourths of all MembersAmendment or revisionMajority of votes cast, plebiscite 60 to 90 days after approval
      Constitutional conventionCalled by two-thirds of all Members, or by majority submitting the question to the votersAmendment or revisionSame
      People’s initiativePetition of 12% of registered voters, at least 3% in every district; not more than once every 5 yearsAmendments onlyPlebiscite 60 to 90 days after COMELEC certifies sufficiency
      Amendment or revision? (Lambino)
      1. Quantitative: is the change so extensive that it alters the substantial entirety of the Constitution?
      2. Qualitative: does it change the basic plan of government (separation of powers, checks and balances; presidential to parliamentary; bicameral to unicameral)?
      If either test is met, it is a revision and cannot be done by initiative.

      Leading cases in order

      1. Gonzales v. COMELEC (1967): Congress as constituent assembly is subject to judicial review; the plebiscite may coincide with a general election.
      2. Tolentino v. COMELEC (1971): all proposals of one convention go to the people together; no piecemeal submission.
      3. Planas and Javellana (1973): the 1973 Constitution was not ratified as the 1935 Constitution required, yet the Court let it stand.
      4. Santiago v. COMELEC (1997): initiative on the Constitution needs an adequate law; RA 6735 is inadequate.
      5. Lambino v. COMELEC (2006): initiative is limited to amendments; the people must author and sign a petition containing the full text.
      Gatmaytan on Javellana (his favorite case): the Court “looked the other way.” A majority found the 1973 Constitution not validly ratified (Citizens’ Assemblies, show of hands, minors voting, martial law), yet dismissed the petitions. In doing so, the Justices removed the judiciary from a position of institutional significance and lost public respect; by 1986 the Court was seen as subservient to Marcos. In ‘Changing Constitutions: Judicial Review and Redemption’, he reads Lambino (2006) as the Court’s redemption: it blocked a government-driven ‘people’s’ initiative despite pressure.
      Exam traps: (1) The vote in Congress is three-fourths of all Members, but the Constitution does not say whether the two chambers vote jointly or separately; the question is open. Argue that bicameralism and the structure of Art. VI support separate voting, and note the contrary reading. (2) An initiative signature sheet without the full text is not a “petition” (Lambino). (3) Santiago’s ruling that RA 6735 is inadequate was not revisited in Lambino, so there is still no adequate enabling law for an initiative on the Constitution.

      A group gathers signatures for a “people’s initiative” to let Congress amend the economic provisions by ordinary law (“unless otherwise provided by law”). Local officials distribute the signature sheets, which describe the change in one sentence. Valid?

      Answer: No. Under Art. XVII, Sec. 2, the people must author and sign the proposal embodied in a petition shown to them in full (Lambino); a one-line summary on a signature sheet does not comply. There is also still no adequate implementing law for initiatives on the Constitution (Santiago v. COMELEC). Finally, if officials drive the campaign, it is not a people’s initiative, the point Gatmaytan stresses in reading Lambino. (Whether letting Congress change economic restrictions by law is an amendment or a revision is arguable; the two defects above are enough.)

      In a news question: a House resolution “calling” for a constituent assembly is not ripe (Lozano v. Nograles). An agreement by the Executive promising constitutional change is grave abuse (North Cotabato). A plebiscite on one proposal ahead of others is barred (Tolentino).

      Judicial review of interpretation questions

      Francisco v. House (2003) is the anchor for both interpretation and justiciability: where the Constitution sets limits on a political branch (the one-year bar on impeachment), the Court must enforce them. “Initiation” means filing plus referral to the Committee on Justice. In re JDF (2015) is the counterpoint: the Court will not rule on a bill.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Three modes, vote thresholds, 60 to 90 days, initiative for amendments only, 12% plus 3% per district, once every 5 years.
      • Lambino’s two tests (quantitative, qualitative) and two requisites (people author and sign; full text in the petition).
      • Santiago: RA 6735 inadequate for constitutional initiatives; still unfixed.
      • Proper submission: same day as election allowed (Gonzales); no piecemeal submission (Tolentino).
      • Javellana’s votes: 6 justiciable, 6 not validly ratified, 6 to dismiss. Gatmaytan: the Court looked the other way.
      • Endencia: Congress cannot interpret the Constitution. Nitafan: framers’ intent controls. Manila Prince: presumption of self-execution.

      Judicial review

      Syllabus III: separation of powers; justification of judicial review; political questions; the four requisites; effects of a ruling. 30 cases. This is the procedural layer of almost every answer.

      Basis: separation of powers and checks and balances

      Art. VIII, Sec. 1The judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law. Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.

      Separation of powers: legislation belongs to Congress, execution to the President, settlement of controversies to the courts. It is violated when one branch (a) impermissibly interferes with another’s function, or (b) assumes a function that belongs to another (Gatmaytan’s book, citing Belgica). Examples: a legislative veto over IRRs (ABAKADA); legislators identifying projects after the budget passes (Belgica); an agency “reviewing” a Supreme Court decision (In re Laureta); a statute interpreting the Constitution (Endencia).

      Angara v. Electoral Commission justifies judicial review: when the Court allocates constitutional boundaries it asserts no superiority but performs its duty, limited to actual cases and the lis mota, with a presumption of constitutionality. Demetria v. Alba: the Court does not interfere while a branch acts within its authority, but must when it exceeds it.

      Gatmaytan: the second paragraph of Sec. 1 (“grave abuse of discretion”) was written because Marcos’s Court hid behind the political question doctrine and earned a reputation as a rubber stamp. Under the 1987 Constitution, “almost every political issue now reaches the Supreme Court.”

      Political questions

      A political question is one which, under the Constitution, is to be decided by the people in their sovereign capacity, or in regard to which full discretionary authority has been given to the legislative or executive branch; it concerns wisdom, not legality. Under the expanded definition, the doctrine is narrow.

      Truly political or justiciable? (Francisco)
      1. Does the Constitution impose limits or conditions on the power exercised (a vote, a time bar, a plebiscite, a procedure)? If yes, whether they were observed is justiciable.
      2. If the matter is left wholly to a political branch’s discretion with no standard, it is truly political; the Court may still ask only whether there was grave abuse.
      • Justiciable: the one-year impeachment bar (Francisco); the plebiscite for converting a city (Miranda v. Aguirre); Congress acting as constituent assembly (Gonzales).
      • Political: choosing a project route on grounds of wisdom (Torrecampo); the factual basis of an urgency certification is generally not reviewed (Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance; Kida).

      The requisites of judicial review

      Four requisites
      1. An actual case or controversy (ripe, not moot).
      2. A proper party with standing (personal and substantial interest; direct injury).
      3. The constitutional question raised at the earliest opportunity.
      4. The constitutional question is the lis mota (necessary to decide the case).

      The syllabus opens the requisites with two cases: KAPIT v. City of Manila (2026), where challenges to the no-contact apprehension ordinances were dismissed as moot and for lack of standing; and White Light (2009), which lists the exceptions to the direct-injury rule and applies third-party standing.

      1. Actual case: ripeness

      The challenged act must have been accomplished and must have a direct adverse effect on the petitioner. Courts do not give advisory opinions.

      • PACU: fear that a regulatory power may be abused is not an injury.
      • Montesclaros: a bill is not a law; no review before enactment.
      • Lozano v. Nograles: a House resolution calling for a constituent assembly is not ripe.
      • PHILCONSA v. Philippine Government (2016): peace agreements needing a law to take effect are not ripe; Congress is not bound by them.

      1. Actual case: mootness

      A case is moot when a supervening event leaves no practical relief. The Court may still decide it if any of the four exceptions applies.

      Exceptions to mootness (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo; Sanlakas)
      1. Grave violation of the Constitution.
      2. Exceptional character and paramount public interest.
      3. The need to formulate controlling principles for the bench, the bar and the public.
      4. Capable of repetition yet evading review.
      • Atlas Fertilizer: mooted by a later ruling and an amendatory law.
      • Lacson v. Perez: lifting the state of rebellion mooted the case.
      • Sanlakas: moot, but decided as capable of repetition.
      • KAPIT (2026): the exceptions apply to the issuance under challenge, not to a successor measure not yet challenged; interest of motorists alone is not ‘paramount public interest’.
      Gatmaytan on Pangilinan v. Cayetano (ICC withdrawal): the Court invented “variant technicalities”: it denied senators standing until the Senate itself acted, and called the case moot because the withdrawal had taken effect. He argues standing of individual legislators was settled, an institutional position should not be required (or a majority could block every challenge by sitting on a resolution), and the case was not moot (an invalid withdrawal could not take effect) and fit every exception.

      2. Proper party (standing)

      General rule (direct injury test): the petitioner suffered an actual or threatened injury from the challenged act, fairly traceable to it, and likely to be redressed by a favorable ruling (AIWA v. Romulo; Joya).

      KindWhen allowedCase
      CitizenEnforcing a public right or duty (publication, information), or transcendental importanceTañada v. Tuvera; Chavez v. PEA
      TaxpayerIllegal disbursement or misuse of public funds, or an unconstitutional taxITF v. COMELEC; not in Joya, AIWA
      VoterObvious interest in the validity of an election law or electionTolentino v. COMELEC (2004)
      LegislatorThe act impairs the prerogatives of Congress or of the legislatorOple v. Torres; Sanlakas
      Association / third partyMembers are injured and the interest is germane to its purpose; or third-party testKMU; Exec. Sec. v. CA; GMA; White Light; CHREA; not in IBP v. Zamora
      GovernmentThe State challenging its own lawPeople v. Vera
      EnvironmentAny citizen as steward of nature under the environmental rulesResident Marine Mammals
      Third-party standing (White Light)
      1. The litigant suffered an injury-in-fact.
      2. The litigant has a close relation to the third party.
      3. Some hindrance prevents the third party from protecting its own interests.

      Transcendental importance can relax standing. Factors used: the character of the funds or assets involved; a clear disregard of a constitutional or statutory prohibition; and the lack of another party with a more direct interest. In IBP v. Zamora, the IBP lacked standing but the Court ruled anyway. In AIWA it refused to relax the rule.

      Gatmaytan on Oposa (‘The Illusion of Intergenerational Equity’): the famous recognition of standing for future generations was obiter, not needed to decide whether the petitioners had a cause of action. Resident Marine Mammals later made animal ‘standing’ unnecessary by pointing to citizen suits under the environmental rules.

      3. Earliest opportunity

      The constitutional issue must be raised at the first chance in the proceedings, in the pleadings before a competent court, not for the first time on appeal (Arceta). It does not mean suing as soon as a law is passed; and a party may challenge a regulation whenever it is enforced against him (Gatmaytan’s book). Falcis (2019): the mere passage of the Family Code created no actual case; filing directly in the Supreme Court without an injury and without a proper respondent failed.

      4. Lis mota

      The constitutional question must be unavoidable; if the case can be decided on another ground, the Court will use that ground (Arceta). This follows from the presumption of constitutionality.

      Effects of a declaration of unconstitutionality

      • Orthodox view (Civil Code, Art. 7): an unconstitutional act confers no rights, imposes no duties, creates no office; it is as if never passed.
      • Operative fact doctrine: acts done in good-faith reliance before the declaration may be respected to avoid injustice. Applied in Araullo (DAP projects that could not be undone, but not to authors without findings of good faith) and in Macalintal (2023) (the October 2023 barangay elections proceeded). Refused where it would reward the beneficiary of the void law (Planters Products v. Fertiphil).
      • Partial unconstitutionality: the valid part stands if separable. A separability clause creates only a presumption.
      Gatmaytan on separability: the Court has lately seemed to require a separability clause to save valid parts (it voided a whole tax ordinance for lacking one). He argues severability should not depend on the clause; that was the Court’s usual approach, and it is the US rule.

      Remedies and forum (quick guide)

      • Certiorari or prohibition under Rule 65 using expanded jurisdiction, filed directly in the Supreme Court for issues of transcendental importance; otherwise mind the hierarchy of courts.
      • Declaratory relief in the RTC for a law not yet violated (Exec. Sec. v. CA; White Light).
      • Electoral disputes: COMELEC before the winner becomes a Member; the HRET or SET after proclamation, oath and assumption; the Supreme Court (as PET) for the President and Vice President.
      • Money claims against the State: COA first (Fetalvero).
      In a news question: write the procedural paragraph in this order: (1) remedy and forum; (2) actual case (is it only a bill, a proposal, a draft IRR?); (3) standing (who is suing, and as what?); (4) mootness if events overtook the case. Then turn to the merits. Two or three lines.

      A party-list representative and a citizens’ group file certiorari in the Supreme Court against a House bill (approved on second reading) that would cap party-list nominees’ age at 60. Should the Court rule on it?

      Answer: No. A bill creates no rights and imposes no duties; ruling on it would be an advisory opinion (Montesclaros; In re JDF). The petition is premature. The representative’s interest as a legislator is not impaired by a bill that is still being debated in her own chamber; her remedy is in the House. The petition should be dismissed without prejudice to a challenge once the measure becomes law.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Four requisites; ripeness (accomplished act plus direct adverse effect); four exceptions to mootness.
      • Standing table: citizen, taxpayer, voter, legislator, association or third party, government, environment; transcendental importance factors.
      • Political question narrowed by Art. VIII, Sec. 1; Francisco test (are there constitutional limits?).
      • Bill or resolution = not ripe (Montesclaros, Lozano, JDF, PHILCONSA 2016).
      • Gatmaytan: Pangilinan’s “variant technicalities”; Oposa obiter; separability should not need a clause.
      • KAPIT (2026): mootness by supervening ordinance; unregistered associations lack capacity; third-party standing needs identified members.

      National territory

      Syllabus IV.A: Art. I; Admin. Code, Book I, Sec. 3; RA 9522 (baselines, 2009); RA 12064 (Maritime Zones Act, 2024); RA 12065 (Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act, 2024); 4 cases and the 2016 Award.

      The provision

      Art. IThe national territory comprises the Philippine archipelago, with all the islands and waters embraced therein, and all other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction, consisting of its terrestrial, fluvial and aerial domains, including its territorial sea, the seabed, the subsoil, the insular shelves, and other submarine areas. The waters around, between, and connecting the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines.

      Two parts: (1) the archipelago with its islands and waters; (2) all other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction. The last sentence states the archipelagic doctrine: waters inside the archipelago are internal waters.

      Territory versus maritime zones

      The key distinction: sovereignty over territory is acquired or lost only by occupation, accretion, cession and prescription; maritime zones under UNCLOS give sovereign rights and jurisdiction measured from baselines. Baselines laws neither add nor lose territory (Magallona).

      ZoneBreadthRights
      Internal / archipelagic watersLandward of baselinesSovereignty (subject to archipelagic sea lanes passage under UNCLOS)
      Territorial sea12 nautical miles from baselinesSovereignty, subject to innocent passage
      Contiguous zone24 nautical miles from baselinesEnforcement of customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws
      Exclusive economic zone200 nautical miles from baselinesSovereign rights over resources; jurisdiction over artificial islands, research, environment
      Continental shelfNatural prolongation, at least 200 nm (up to 350 nm in some cases)Sovereign rights over seabed resources
      • RA 9522 (baselines): treats the Kalayaan Island Group and Scarborough Shoal as a ‘regime of islands’ under UNCLOS Art. 121, outside the main baselines, without giving up any claim.
      • RA 12064 (Maritime Zones Act, 2024): defines the maritime zones in domestic law consistent with UNCLOS and the 2016 Award.
      • RA 12065 (Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act, 2024): designates sea lanes through which foreign ships and aircraft exercise archipelagic sea lanes passage.

      Cases

      1. Magallona v. Ermita (2011): RA 9522 valid; UNCLOS is a treaty on sea-use rights, not on acquiring territory.
      2. South China Sea Arbitration (2016): China’s nine-dash-line historic rights invalid beyond UNCLOS; no Spratly feature generates an EEZ; China violated Philippine sovereign rights. The tribunal did not decide sovereignty over features.
      3. North Cotabato v. GRP (2008): the MOA-AD’s associative ‘Bangsamoro Juridical Entity’ and the promise to change the Constitution were unconstitutional.
      4. Cruz v. DENR (2000): IPRA survived a 7–7 vote; native title versus the Regalian Doctrine.
      In a news question: West Philippine Sea incidents (water cannons, blocking resupply, reclamation): the question is usually about sovereign rights in the EEZ under UNCLOS and the Award, not ‘territory’. For a government agreement on joint exploration, add Art. XII, Sec. 2 (exploration of natural resources under full State control and supervision) and the treaty concurrence rule if it is an international agreement.
      Exam trap: saying RA 9522 ‘gave up’ Kalayaan or Scarborough. It did not; it classified them as a regime of islands, which preserves the claim and is consistent with UNCLOS.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Territory is acquired only by occupation, accretion, cession, prescription; baselines and UNCLOS do not change it.
      • Zones: 12, 24, 200 nautical miles; continental shelf.
      • Award (2016): historic rights extinguished to the extent incompatible with UNCLOS; Spratly features cannot generate an EEZ.
      • MOA-AD: the President cannot guarantee constitutional amendments.

      Citizenship

      Syllabus IV.B.1: Art. IV; Admin. Code, Book I, Secs. 5–9; RA 9139; RA 8171; RA 9225. 17 cases. Tested in 2015 (Poe; citizenship by statute) and 2016 (dual citizens in government).

      The provisions

      Art. IV, Secs. 1 to 5Section 1. The following are citizens of the Philippines: (1) Those who are citizens of the Philippines at the time of the adoption of this Constitution; (2) Those whose fathers or mothers are citizens of the Philippines; (3) Those born before January 17, 1973, of Filipino mothers, who elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching the age of majority; and (4) Those who are naturalized in accordance with law.
      Section 2. Natural-born citizens are those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship. Those who elect Philippine citizenship in accordance with paragraph (3), Section 1 hereof shall be deemed natural-born citizens.
      Section 3. Philippine citizenship may be lost or reacquired in the manner provided by law.
      Section 4. Citizens of the Philippines who marry aliens shall retain their citizenship, unless by their act or omission, they are deemed, under the law, to have renounced it.
      Section 5. Dual allegiance of citizens is inimical to the national interest and shall be dealt with by law.

      Natural-born or naturalized

      The Philippines follows jus sanguinis. A natural-born citizen needs no act to acquire or perfect citizenship. Everyone else is naturalized, except those who elect under Sec. 1(3), who are deemed natural-born.

      • Tecson (2004): an illegitimate child of a Filipino father is Filipino if filiation is proved.
      • David v. SET (2016): foundlings are natural-born.
      • Co v. HRET (1991): election may be implied from acts (voting, holding office) for those already treated as Filipino.
      • Republic v. Sagun (2012): formal election under CA 625 needs a sworn statement, oath, and registration within a reasonable time (about 3 years).
      • Bengson v. Cruz (2001): repatriation restores natural-born status.
      OfficeCitizenship required
      President, Vice President, Senator, Member of the HouseNatural-born (Arts. VI and VII)
      Justices of the Supreme Court and lower collegiate courts; members of constitutional commissions; Ombudsman and deputies; Monetary Board members (majority from private sector)Natural-born (Constitution)
      RTC and other lower court judgesNatural-born (by law: BP 129 as amended; see RA 11459 on Judges-at-Large)
      Local elective officials‘Citizen of the Philippines’ (LGC, Sec. 39); naturalized citizens qualify

      Naturalization

      • Judicial (CA 473): strict compliance; privilege, not a right. Go v. Republic (credible witnesses; petition contents), Go Pei Hung (certificate of arrival), Mahtani (lucrative occupation).
      • Administrative (RA 9139, 2000): for aliens born and residing in the Philippines since birth, through a Special Committee on Naturalization.
      • Legislative: Congress may naturalize a person by a law (a private bill, originating in the House under Art. VI, Sec. 24). The person is naturalized, not natural-born.
      • Derivative: minor children of a naturalized father (Tan Co).
      Exam trap (2015 midterm, RA 10685 for Peter Wallace): a person naturalized by statute cannot be a Senator or Supreme Court Justice (natural-born required). For a local office, the LGC requires only citizenship plus residence and the other qualifications, so the strongest answer is that he may run for local office if he has those qualifications. The circulated key marked ‘none of the above’; see the item note in the Past exams tab.

      Loss and reacquisition

      • Lost by naturalization abroad, express renunciation, oath to another country, and other grounds under CA 63. Conduct can be express renunciation (Willie Yu).
      • Reacquired by naturalization, repatriation (RA 8171; PD 725; RA 2630) or under RA 9225. Repatriation is filed with the Special Committee on Naturalization, not the RTC (Angat). It retroacts to the application (Frivaldo).

      Dual citizenship and RA 9225

      Dual citizenship (arising from the concurrent laws of two States, often by birth) is not dual allegiance (a positive act of loyalty to another State). Art. IV, Sec. 5 leaves dual allegiance to Congress (Calilung).

      RA 9225 for candidates (Sobejana-Condon; Chua; Maquiling)
      1. Take the oath of allegiance (to reacquire or retain citizenship).
      2. For elective office: make a personal and sworn renunciation of all foreign citizenship before an officer authorized to administer oaths, at the latest when filing the COC.
      3. Keep acting consistently: using a foreign passport after renouncing recants the renunciation (Maquiling).
      For appointive office, RA 9225 requires the appointee to renounce foreign citizenship before an authorized officer before assuming office (and to meet the office’s other qualifications).

      These steps apply only to those who reacquired citizenship after naturalization abroad. A dual citizen by birth need not renounce; filing the COC is itself a renunciation (Gana-Carait, 2022).

      Update (2025): when a winner is disqualified, Maquiling and Chua proclaimed the next-ranked qualified candidate. Mangudadatu v. COMELEC (2025) abandoned that rule; the vacancy is now filled by succession (e.g., the vice-mayor or vice-governor).
      In a news question (2016 midterm, CSC barring dual citizens): an agency cannot bar dual citizens from government service by memorandum; Art. IV, Sec. 5 leaves dual allegiance to Congress, and RA 9225 already provides the conditions (renunciation for public office). The CSC lacks authority to add a disqualification (Calilung).
      Gatmaytan: his article ‘Hard Cases Make Bad Movies’ (2021) on the Poe cases is assigned under both citizenship and the presidency. His 2015 exam asked about forum (COMELEC before the election; SET for a sitting senator; PET after a presidential election) and whether two tribunals may reach different results.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Four classes of citizens; natural-born definition; Jan. 17, 1973 election rule.
      • Offices requiring natural-born status; local office needs only citizenship.
      • Three modes of naturalization; strict compliance.
      • RA 9225: oath, then sworn personal renunciation (candidates); passport use recants; dual by birth exempt (Gana-Carait).
      • Repatriation restores natural-born status (Bengson); retroacts (Frivaldo); filed with the Special Committee (Angat).
      • Second-placer rule abandoned (Mangudadatu, 2025).

      Suffrage

      Syllabus IV.B.2: Art. V; RA 9189 as amended by RA 10590 (overseas voting); 7 cases. Tested in the 2015 finals (No Bio, No Boto; registration deadline).

      The provisions

      Art. V, Secs. 1 and 2Section 1. Suffrage may be exercised by all citizens of the Philippines, not otherwise disqualified by law, who are at least eighteen years of age, and who shall have resided in the Philippines for at least one year and in the place wherein they propose to vote, for at least six months immediately preceding the election. No literacy, property, or other substantive requirement shall be imposed on the exercise of suffrage.
      Section 2. The Congress shall provide a system for securing the secrecy and sanctity of the ballot as well as a system for absentee voting by qualified Filipinos abroad. The Congress shall also design a procedure for the disabled and the illiterates to vote without the assistance of other persons. Until then, they shall be allowed to vote under existing laws and such rules as the Commission on Elections may promulgate to protect the secrecy of the ballot.

      Qualifications versus regulation

      Qualifications are fixed by the Constitution: citizenship, age 18, one year in the Philippines and six months in the place of voting. Congress may disqualify (“not otherwise disqualified by law”) but cannot impose a literacy, property, or other substantive requirement. Registration is not a qualification; it is the procedure by which qualifications are determined, and may be reasonably regulated.

      Is the new condition valid?
      1. Is it a qualification or a substantive requirement (e.g., passing a test, paying a fee, owning property)? If so, invalid.
      2. Is it part of registration or procedure? Valid if reasonable. Where it burdens the fundamental right, apply strict scrutiny: compelling interest and least restrictive means (Kabataan).
      3. Was it made by the right body? COMELEC must stay within the law (Palatino).
      • Kabataan v. COMELEC (2015): biometrics validation is registration, not a qualification; passes strict scrutiny.
      • AKBAYAN v. COMELEC (2001): no special registration within the 120-day prohibitive period.
      • Palatino v. COMELEC (2009): COMELEC cannot close registration earlier than the law allows unless it shows the pre-election acts cannot reasonably be done; deadline voided.
      • Ceniza v. COMELEC (1980): HUC voters may be excluded from provincial elections; reasonable classification.
      • Macalintal v. COMELEC (2003): overseas absentee voting is an exception to the residence requirement; the affidavit of intent to return is valid.

      Residence

      Residence in election law means domicile. A new domicile requires bodily presence, intent to remain, and intent to abandon the old (Gallego v. Verra). Absence for work or study, or forced exile, does not lose domicile (Romualdez v. RTC). The same rule governs candidates (Aquino; Marcos; Mangudadatu).

      In a news question: COMELEC deactivations, registration deadlines, voting fees, ID requirements, or proposals to bar some group from voting. Ask: qualification or regulation? Which body acted, and within what law? Is it inside the 120-day (regular) or 90-day (special) prohibitive period?

      COMELEC sets the registration deadline for the May 2028 elections on September 30, 2027, citing the new automated system, and suspends registration for a week during the filing of COCs. Valid?

      Answer: Not without proof. RA 8189, Sec. 8 allows continuing registration until 120 days before a regular election. COMELEC’s stand-by power to fix other dates applies only if the pre-election acts cannot reasonably be done within that period, which it must show (Palatino; AKBAYAN). Administrative convenience during COC filing is not enough. The deadline and suspension should be set aside unless COMELEC proves necessity.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Qualifications: citizen, 18, 1 year in the Philippines, 6 months in the place.
      • No literacy, property, or other substantive requirement; registration is procedure.
      • 120 days (regular) / 90 days (special) no-registration period; Palatino versus AKBAYAN.
      • Domicile: presence, animus manendi, animus non revertendi.
      • Overseas voting is an exception to residence (Macalintal 2003); a JCOC approving COMELEC rules is invalid.

      Government, state immunity, and the inherent powers

      Syllabus IV.C: government defined; governmental functions; de facto, de jure and revolutionary government; parens patriae; immunity from suit; money claims; police power. 15 cases. Police power over private businesses was asked in 2023 (cinema free screen time) and 2024 (entrance exam fee waiver).

      Government and its functions

      • ‘Government’ is the system and institutions, distinct from the persons administering it (U.S. v. Dorr). Criticism of officials is not an attack on the government.
      • ‘Government of the Philippines’ (Admin. Code, Sec. 2(1)): the corporate governmental entity through which governmental functions are exercised, including its political subdivisions.
      • Constituent functions (compulsory: order, justice, property, contracts) and ministrant functions (optional: welfare, public works) are no longer sharply distinguished. A public office: created by law, delegated sovereign power, continuing, defined by law, for the public benefit (Laurel v. Desierto).

      De jure, de facto and revolutionary governments

      Three kinds of de facto government (Co Kim Cham): (1) one that usurps the legitimate government by force or the majority’s will; (2) one established by an invading military force (paramount force); (3) one set up by insurgents who secede. Acts of a de facto government not of a political complexion remain valid after restoration (postliminy).

      A revolutionary government is bound by no constitution, but the Aquino revolutionary government remained bound by the ICCPR and the Universal Declaration (Republic v. Sandiganbayan).

      In a news question: calls for a ‘revolutionary government’ by a sitting president: he was elected under the 1987 Constitution; declaring one repudiates the Constitution that gives him office. Nothing in the Constitution authorizes it.

      Parens patriae

      The State may protect those who cannot protect themselves (minors, incompetents), but it supplements, not replaces, parents. Restrictions on minors’ fundamental rights are reviewed by strict scrutiny (SPARK v. Quezon City): compelling interest plus least restrictive means.

      Immunity from suit

      Art. XVI, Sec. 3The State may not be sued without its consent.
      Analysis
      1. Is it really a suit against the State? A suit against an officer is against the State if a judgment would require the State to pay or act (Arigo). Not if the officer acted beyond authority, the relief is only to nullify an ultra vires act, or the officer is sued personally for a tort (PASI v. Trinidad-Lichauco).
      2. Has the State consented? Expressly by law, or impliedly when it sues or enters into a commercial (jure gestionis) contract. Incorporated agencies: look at the charter (‘sue and be sued’) (GTZ).
      3. Foreign States and their agents: restrictive immunity covers sovereign acts (jure imperii). Agents acting within official functions, with the host State’s consent, share immunity (Minucher). Warships are immune; the flag State answers internationally (Arigo).
      4. Suability is not liability: even if the State may be sued, public funds cannot be garnished; claims go to COA (Fetalvero). But immunity cannot be used to avoid paying for a completed public work the State has used (Vigilar).

      Inherent powers: police power, eminent domain, taxation

      Police power is the State’s power to restrain liberty and property to promote the general welfare. It needs no constitutional grant; Congress holds it and delegates it to the President, agencies and LGUs (general welfare clause).

      Valid police power (lawful subject and lawful means)
      1. Lawful subject: the interests of the public generally, not of a particular class, require the interference.
      2. Lawful means: the means are reasonably necessary to the purpose and not unduly oppressive on individuals.
      For LGUs: the ordinance must also be within the delegated power, consistent with law, and not prohibit (as opposed to regulate) a lawful business (Cruz v. Paras; White Light).
      • Upheld: Mangyan reservation (Rubi, 1919); early warning devices (Agustin v. Edu); Boracay closure (Zabal); expanding a power distributor’s franchise into cooperatives’ areas (Iloilo I Electric Coop., 2024: franchises are never exclusive and yield to the common good).
      • Struck down: short-time motel rates ban (White Light); curfews not narrowly drawn (SPARK).

      Regulation or taking?

      Police power regulates the use of property without compensation; eminent domain takes property (or its use) for public use and requires just compensation. A regulation becomes a taking when it appropriates property or its beneficial use for the public, rather than restraining a noxious or harmful use.

      MeasureClassification
      Requiring cemeteries to set aside 6% of their land for paupers (City Government of QC v. Ericta, 1983)Taking without compensation (void)
      Requiring newspapers to give COMELEC free print space (Philippine Press Institute v. COMELEC, 1995)Taking; must be paid for
      Requiring broadcasters to give COMELEC free airtime (TELEBAP v. COMELEC, 1998)Valid: broadcasters hold franchises over a public resource (airwaves) and the condition is part of the privilege
      Senior citizens’ and PWD discounts, deductible from income (Manila Memorial Park v. DSWD, 2013)Valid police power
      In a news question (2023: Manila cinemas must give free screen time for city messages; 2024: private HEIs must waive entrance exam fees): (1) Lawful subject? Public information or access to education is a legitimate public interest. (2) Lawful means? Is the burden reasonable and spread fairly, or does it appropriate the private owner’s property (screen time, services) for public use without pay? Cinemas, unlike broadcasters, hold no franchise over a public resource, so PPI and Ericta point to a taking. For schools, add Art. XIV, Sec. 4(1) (reasonable supervision and regulation of educational institutions) and ask whether the waived fee is a modest regulation of a regulated business or an uncompensated appropriation of its services. Answer either way, but apply both tests to the exact words.
      Exam trap: calling every burden on a business ‘police power’. Ask whether the State is restraining a use or taking something for public use. Also: non-impairment yields to police power (Iloilo I), but only to a valid exercise of it.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Dorr: government versus administration. Laurel: elements of public office.
      • Three kinds of de facto government; postliminy; revolutionary government still bound by human rights instruments.
      • SPARK: parens patriae plus strict scrutiny.
      • Immunity: suit against the State? consent? foreign agent? suability is not liability; COA for money claims.
      • Police power: lawful subject plus lawful means; regulation versus taking (Ericta, PPI, TELEBAP).

      Congress: composition, party-list, qualifications and elections

      Syllabus V.A.1–2: Art. VI, Secs. 1 to 9; RA 7941; RA 6645 and RA 7166; 18 cases. Tested in 2024 (party-list proposals) and 2023 (adding qualifications through a ‘debate’ requirement).

      The provisions

      Art. VI, Secs. 3, 5(1)–(2), 6Section 3. No person shall be a Senator unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines and, on the day of the election, is at least thirty-five years of age, able to read and write, a registered voter, and a resident of the Philippines for not less than two years immediately preceding the day of the election.
      Section 5. (1) The House of Representatives shall be composed of not more than two hundred and fifty members, unless otherwise fixed by law, who shall be elected from legislative districts apportioned among the provinces, cities, and the Metropolitan Manila area in accordance with the number of their respective inhabitants, and on the basis of a uniform and progressive ratio, and those who, as provided by law, shall be elected through a party-list system of registered national, regional, and sectoral parties or organizations. (2) The party-list representatives shall constitute twenty per centum of the total number of representatives including those under the party list. For three consecutive terms after the ratification of this Constitution, one-half of the seats allocated to party-list representatives shall be filled, as provided by law, by selection or election from the labor, peasant, urban poor, indigenous cultural communities, women, youth, and such other sectors as may be provided by law, except the religious sector.
      Section 6. No person shall be a Member of the House of Representatives unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines and, on the day of the election, is at least twenty-five years of age, able to read and write, and, except the party-list representatives, a registered voter in the district in which he shall be elected, and a resident thereof for a period of not less than one year immediately preceding the day of the election.

      Qualifications cannot be added by law

      The qualifications in Secs. 3 and 6 are exclusive. Congress cannot add to them by statute, directly or indirectly. In Social Justice Society v. Dangerous Drugs Board (2008), cited in Gatmaytan’s book, mandatory drug testing of senatorial candidates was void because it added a qualification. The same reasoning applies to any law that ‘disqualifies’ candidates who do something (or fail to do something) not listed in the Constitution.

      In a news question (2023 Q4: a law disqualifying candidates who skip COMELEC debates): for President, Vice President, Senators and Representatives, the qualifications are fixed by the Constitution; disqualifying a candidate for skipping debates adds a qualification and is void (SJS v. DDB; Endencia’s logic that Congress cannot alter the Constitution by statute). For local offices, the qualifications are statutory, so Congress has more room, but the condition must still be reasonable and not burden suffrage arbitrarily (Albano; Macalintal 2023). Also mention free speech: a candidate cannot be compelled to speak.
      SenatorRepresentative (district)Party-list nominee
      CitizenshipNatural-bornNatural-bornNatural-born
      Age (election day)352525 (RA 7941; youth sector nominees 25 to 30)
      LiteracyRead and writeRead and writeRead and write
      Voter registrationRegistered voterIn the districtRegistered voter (RA 7941)
      Residence2 years in the Philippines1 year in the district1 year in the Philippines, bona fide member of the party for 90 days (RA 7941)
      Term / limit6 years / 2 consecutive3 years / 3 consecutive3 years / 3 consecutive

      Residence means domicile (Aquino; Marcos). A sitting official who keeps performing his office elsewhere cannot claim a new domicile (Mangudadatu, 2025).

      Update (2025): Mangudadatu abandoned the second-placer rule: when a winning candidate is disqualified, the next-ranked candidate is no longer proclaimed; the office is filled by succession.

      Legislative districts

      • Districts: contiguous, compact and adjacent territory; every city of 250,000 and every province gets at least one representative; reapportionment within three years after each census (Sec. 5(3)–(4)).
      • The House may exceed 250 by law, including piecemeal laws creating districts (Mariano v. COMELEC; BANAT, cited in Gatmaytan’s book).
      • Only Congress can create districts, so only Congress can create provinces and cities; the ARMM assembly could not (Sema).

      The party-list system

      Party-list representatives are 20% of the House, ‘as provided by law’ (RA 7941). The evolution:

      1. Ang Bagong Bayani (2001): the system is for the marginalized and underrepresented.
      2. Atong Paglaum (2013): abandoned that reading; national, regional and sectoral parties may join; national and regional parties need not be marginalized (six parameters on its card).
      3. Later cases apply Atong Paglaum: no track record required of the group (Abang Lingkod); no exclusion on moral grounds (Ang Ladlad).
      4. Albano (2023): Congress may set nominee qualifications, but they must pass equal protection; the ban on losing candidates was void.
      Seat allocation (BANAT, as refined)
      1. Rank groups by votes; divisor is total valid party-list votes, including votes for groups on the ballot later disqualified (Araro).
      2. Each group with at least 2% gets one guaranteed seat.
      3. Remaining seats: multiply each group’s percentage by the remaining seats; whole numbers are additional seats; then one seat each down the ranking until filled. No 2% threshold in this round (AKMA-PTM).
      4. Maximum of three seats per group.

      Who decides what

      DisputeForumCase
      Registration and cancellation of the group (even with a sitting member)COMELECAn Waray (2024); due process required (Senior Citizens)
      Internal leadership and nominations before assumptionCOMELECLokin
      Substitution of nomineesCOMELEC, applying mandatory deadlinesDuterte Youth (2024)
      Qualifications or expulsion of a sitting memberHRETLico
      In a news question (2024 Q1: COMELEC chair’s proposals to amend the party-list law): Congress may amend RA 7941 because Sec. 5(1)–(2) leaves the system ‘as provided by law’. But (1) it cannot exclude national and regional parties or limit the system to the marginalized if that reading of the Constitution stands (Atong Paglaum held the framers did not intend an exclusively sectoral system); (2) any restriction on nominees (e.g., must be members of the sector) must have a rational basis under equal protection (Albano); (3) COMELEC cannot impose these by resolution; and (4) a proposal is not ripe for review until enacted.

      Elections and vacancies

      • Regular elections: second Monday of May unless otherwise provided by law. ‘Unless otherwise provided by law’ means a law fixing another date or delegating it to COMELEC; COMELEC cannot suspend an election on its own (Bañas-Nograles).
      • Vacancies (Sec. 9): a special election ‘may be called … in the manner prescribed by law’; the winner serves only the unexpired term. Senate: with the next regular election (Tolentino, 2004). House: COMELEC must call it 60 to 90 days after the vacancy (if at least one year remains) without waiting for a House resolution (Hagedorn, 2025).

      Last-minute checklist

      • Qualifications table; they cannot be added by law (SJS v. DDB).
      • Atong Paglaum’s parameters; Albano (Congress can legislate, but rationally); Duterte Youth (substitution deadlines; voters’ right to know nominees).
      • COMELEC (group, nominations) versus HRET (sitting member).
      • Seat formula: 2%, guaranteed seat, proportional additional seats, cap of 3; divisor per Araro.
      • Special elections: Senate with next regular election; House 60 to 90 days, COMELEC calls (Hagedorn).
      • Second-placer rule abandoned (Mangudadatu).

      Congress: officers, quorum, rules, discipline and the Journal

      Syllabus V.A.3: Art. VI, Secs. 15 and 16; 16 cases. Tested in 2023 (Teves expulsion), 2013 (counting a hospitalized member for quorum), 2015 finals (absentee members and the Ombudsman).

      The provisions

      Art. VI, Sec. 16(1) The Senate shall elect its President and the House of Representatives, its Speaker, by a majority vote of all its respective Members. Each House shall choose such other officers as it may deem necessary.
      (2) A majority of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business, but a smaller number may adjourn from day to day and may compel the attendance of absent Members in such manner, and under such penalties, as such House may provide.
      (3) Each House may determine the rules of its proceedings, punish its Members for disorderly behavior, and, with the concurrence of two-thirds of all its Members, suspend or expel a Member. A penalty of suspension, when imposed, shall not exceed sixty days.
      (4) Each House shall keep a Journal of its proceedings, and from time to time publish the same, excepting such parts as may, in its judgment, affect national security; and the yeas and nays on any question shall, at the request of one-fifth of the Members present, be entered in the Journal. Each House shall also keep a Record of its proceedings.
      (5) Neither House during the sessions of the Congress shall, without the consent of the other, adjourn for more than three days, nor to any other place than that in which the two Houses shall be sitting.

      Officers and internal rules

      • Only the Senate President and Speaker are constitutionally elected (majority of all Members). Everything else (minority leader, committee chairs) is for the chamber (Santiago v. Guingona; Baguilat).
      • Courts do not enforce purely internal rules (Arroyo v. De Venecia), except when (a) a constitutional requirement is involved (quorum, voting, publication: Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole), or (b) third parties’ rights are affected (Pacete).

      Quorum

      A majority of the members within the coercive jurisdiction of the chamber (Avelino v. Cuenco: 12 of 23 senators present in the country). Quorum is presumed to continue unless challenged through the chamber’s procedure; the Journal and the enrolled bill control (Tinio v. Duterte, 2023).

      2013 midterm (Dimaporo in hospital detention): he remains a Member and is counted in the base for computing the majority of the House; whether he is ‘present’ for quorum is a different question. Members cannot be compelled to attend while lawfully detained (Jalosjos). Read the question’s exact verb (‘counted as a member’ versus ‘counted as present’).
      In a news question (2015 finals: Ombudsman asked to compel absent members to attend): Sec. 16(2) gives each House the power to compel attendance of absent members ‘in such manner, and under such penalties, as such House may provide’. The remedy is internal. The Ombudsman cannot intrude into a constitutional function of Congress; separation of powers. Members’ salaries are fixed by law, so absence alone does not create a disallowance unless a rule provides a penalty.

      Discipline of members

      Valid suspension or expulsion
      1. Ground: disorderly behavior, as the House determines (wide deference: Osmeña v. Pendatun).
      2. Vote: two-thirds of all Members (not just those present).
      3. Suspension: not more than 60 days. Expulsion has no cap but is the gravest penalty.
      4. Due process: notice and a chance to be heard (Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole).
      5. No conviction required; it is distinct from criminal liability.
      • Alejandrino (1924): courts would not order reinstatement of a suspended senator (decided before the 60-day cap).
      • Osmeña (1960): the speech privilege does not shield a member from his own House; taking up other business does not waive discipline.
      • De Venecia v. Sandiganbayan (2002): a court’s preventive suspension under RA 3019 is not discipline and is valid.
      • Pobre v. Defensor-Santiago (2009): discipline for floor speech belongs to the chamber, not the courts.
      In a news question (2023 Q1, Teves): no conviction is needed and the Court defers on what is disorderly. But you can argue for him: (1) the House already suspended him twice for 60 days for the same absence, so expelling him for it evades the cap and punishes twice; (2) grounds like a terrorist designation by the Executive and a personal video are not disorderly behavior as a Member; (3) due process. Know both sides.

      Journal, Record and the enrolled bill

      RuleContentCase
      Enrolled bill doctrineThe signatures of the Senate President and Speaker and the secretaries’ certification are conclusive of due enactmentCoTeSCUP (2018); Tinio (2023); Arroyo v. De Venecia
      Probative value of the JournalConclusive on what it records; no extrinsic evidenceU.S. v. Pons
      Journal over enrolled billOnly for matters the Constitution requires in the Journal (yeas and nays on third reading and on veto override, veto messages, yeas and nays on request of one-fifth)Morales v. Subido
      ExceptionIf the presiding officers withdraw their signatures because the enrolled text is wrong, there is no enrolled bill; consult the JournalAstorga v. Villegas

      Sessions: regular session from the fourth Monday of July until 30 days before the next opening (Sec. 15); the President may call special sessions; joint sessions for war, canvassing presidential votes, martial law revocation or extension, and the SONA.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Speaker and Senate President: majority of all Members; other officers per chamber rules.
      • Quorum: majority within coercive jurisdiction (Avelino); presumed to continue (Tinio).
      • Discipline: disorderly behavior; two-thirds of all Members; suspension max 60 days; no conviction needed.
      • Internal rules not enforced by courts, except constitutional requirements or third-party rights.
      • Enrolled bill conclusive; Astorga exception; Journal for constitutionally required entries.

      Congress: salaries, privileges and disqualifications

      Syllabus V.A.4: Art. VI, Secs. 10 to 14; RA 10530; 11 cases. Tested in 2024 (Liban and RA 10530) and 2013 (arrest of a congressman).

      The provisions

      Art. VI, Secs. 10, 11, 13, 14Section 10. The salaries of Senators and Members of the House of Representatives shall be determined by law. No increase in said compensation shall take effect until after the expiration of the full term of all the Members of the Senate and the House of Representatives approving such increase.
      Section 11. A Senator or Member of the House of Representatives shall, in all offenses punishable by not more than six years imprisonment, be privileged from arrest while the Congress is in session. No Member shall be questioned nor be held liable in any other place for any speech or debate in the Congress or in any committee thereof.
      Section 13. No Senator or Member of the House of Representatives may hold any other office or employment in the Government, or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries, during his term without forfeiting his seat. Neither shall he be appointed to any office which may have been created or the emoluments thereof increased during the term for which he was elected.
      Section 14. No Senator or Member of the House of Representatives may personally appear as counsel before any court of justice or before the Electoral Tribunals, or quasi-judicial and other administrative bodies. Neither shall he, directly or indirectly, be interested financially in any contract with, or in any franchise or special privilege granted by the Government, or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including any government-owned or controlled corporation, or its subsidiary, during his term of office. He shall not intervene in any matter before any office of the Government for his pecuniary benefit or where he may be called upon to act on account of his office.

      Salaries

      An increase takes effect only after the full term of all members of both Houses who approved it has expired (PHILCONSA v. Mathay). It cannot be achieved indirectly through retirement benefits (Ligot v. Mathay).

      Freedom from arrest

      Privilege applies only if
      1. the offense is punishable by not more than six years’ imprisonment; and
      2. Congress is in session (regular or special, not recess).
      It does not cover offenses punishable by more than six years, and it never exempts a convicted or lawfully detained member (Jalosjos; Trillanes v. Pimentel).
      2013 midterm (Dimaporo, malversation punishable by more than 6 years, arrested in hospital): the arrest is legal; the privilege covers only offenses punishable by not more than six years. A detained member may be counted in computing the House’s membership but cannot insist on attending sessions (Jalosjos).

      Speech and debate

      The privilege covers utterances and acts in the performance of legislative functions: floor speeches, votes, bills, committee proceedings (Jimenez v. Cabangbang). It does not cover press releases, open letters or media interviews (Jimenez; Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen). It protects against being questioned ‘in any other place’, not against the member’s own chamber (Osmeña) or against the chamber’s discipline (Pobre).

      Incompatible and forbidden offices

      Incompatible office (first sentence)Forbidden office (second sentence)
      Which officesAny other office or employment in the government, its subdivisions, agencies, instrumentalities, GOCCs and subsidiariesAny office created, or whose emoluments were increased, during the term for which he was elected
      EffectHe may accept, but forfeits his seat (Adaza)He cannot be appointed at all during that term, even if he resigns

      Liban v. Gordon: the PNRC chairmanship is not a government office (the PNRC is sui generis, an auxiliary of government, not a GOCC), so a senator who chairs it keeps his seat. The 2009 ruling that RA 95 was unconstitutional (Congress cannot create a private corporation by special charter, Art. XII, Sec. 16) was reversed in 2011 because it was not the lis mota and the PNRC is not an ordinary private corporation.

      2024 Q4: how RA 10530 answers Liban. Liban raised: (1) is the PNRC a GOCC (so a legislator chairing it forfeits his seat)? (2) can Congress create the PNRC by special charter when Art. XII, Sec. 16 bars special charters for private corporations? RA 10530 (2013) settles both by statute: it recognizes the PNRC as an independent, autonomous, non-governmental organization auxiliary to the authorities of the Government in the humanitarian field, consistent with the Geneva Conventions. It is neither a GOCC nor a private corporation formed for profit, so (1) its chairmanship is not a government office under Sec. 13, and (2) its charter is not barred by Art. XII, Sec. 16. Mention that the 2011 Resolution had already called the PNRC sui generis; RA 10530 codifies it.

      Sec. 14: no personal appearance as counsel before courts, tribunals or administrative bodies; this cannot be evaded by buying shares to intervene as a ‘stockholder’ (Puyat v. De Guzman). A detained senator-petitioner’s request to argue her own case was denied (Pangilinan v. Cayetano, Notice, 2018).

      Sec. 12 (disclosure of financial interests and conflicts of interest) and Sec. 20 (COA audit of Congress’s books, with an annual itemized list of amounts paid to each Member) complete the accountability provisions.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Salary increase: after the full term of all members of both Houses who approved it.
      • Arrest privilege: offenses up to 6 years, while in session; not for detention after charge for graver crimes or conviction.
      • Speech: legislative acts only; not media; not immunity from one’s own chamber.
      • Incompatible (forfeits seat) versus forbidden (cannot be appointed) offices.
      • Liban 2009 and 2011; RA 10530: PNRC is independent, autonomous, non-governmental, auxiliary to government.

      Electoral tribunals and the Commission on Appointments

      Syllabus V.A.5–6: Art. VI, Secs. 17 to 19; 12 cases. Tested in 2013 (Muhlach v. Fuentebella: COMELEC or HRET?) and 2015 (Poe: forum).

      The provisions

      Art. VI, Secs. 17 and 18Section 17. The Senate and the House of Representatives shall each have an Electoral Tribunal which shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of their respective Members. Each Electoral Tribunal shall be composed of nine Members, three of whom shall be Justices of the Supreme Court to be designated by the Chief Justice, and the remaining six shall be Members of the Senate or the House of Representatives, as the case may be, who shall be chosen on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties and the parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein. The senior Justice in the Electoral Tribunal shall be its Chairman.
      Section 18. There shall be a Commission on Appointments consisting of the President of the Senate, as ex officio Chairman, twelve Senators, and twelve Members of the House of Representatives, elected by each House on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties and parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein. The chairman of the Commission shall not vote, except in case of a tie. The Commission shall act on all appointments submitted to it within thirty session days of the Congress from their submission. The Commission shall rule by a majority vote of all the Members.

      When does the tribunal take over from COMELEC?

      HRET or SET jurisdiction begins when three things concur (Reyes v. COMELEC, 2013)
      1. A valid proclamation;
      2. a proper oath (for the House, before the Speaker in open session);
      3. assumption of office (on June 30).
      Before that, COMELEC keeps jurisdiction over the winner’s qualifications. If COMELEC’s ruling on the proclamation itself is still pending, the tribunal does not acquire jurisdiction (Codilla). If the COC was finally cancelled before the election, there is no ‘member’ for the tribunal to judge (Velasco).
      2013 midterm (Muhlach v. Fuentebella): Fuentebella had been proclaimed; Muhlach’s remedy is an election protest in the HRET once Fuentebella becomes a member (proclamation, oath, assumption). Before assumption, Reyes v. COMELEC says COMELEC still has jurisdiction, so read the dates. The circulated key chose the HRET.

      Nature of the tribunals

      • ‘Sole judge’: independent of the chamber and of the courts; non-partisan (‘a non-political body in a sea of politicians’, Gatmaytan’s book).
      • Members have security of tenure; a chamber cannot remove a member for voting against his party (Bondoc v. Pineda). Valid causes: end of term, death or disability, resignation from the party he represents, formal affiliation with another party, removal for other valid cause.
      • All members must sit; the Justices alone cannot decide (Abbas). A rule requiring at least one Justice for a quorum is valid (Reyes v. HRET).
      • The Supreme Court reviews tribunal decisions only for grave abuse (e.g., annulling precincts without substantial evidence: Abayon).
      • Each chamber chooses its members of the tribunal and the CA; claimants go to the chamber first (Pimentel v. HRET).

      Commission on Appointments

      Proportional representation in the CA
      1. Senate seats per party = (party’s senators ÷ 24) × 12; House seats computed the same way on the House membership.
      2. Fractions cannot be rounded up at another party’s expense (Guingona v. Gonzales); the CA can function with fewer than 12 from a chamber.
      3. A party must be big enough for at least one seat; being ‘minority’ is not enough (Coseteng).
      4. Membership may be changed when political alignments change permanently (Daza v. Singson), not for temporary alliances.
      5. Challengers must have standing and first raise the matter in the chamber (Drilon v. De Venecia).

      The CA confirms the appointments listed in Art. VII, Sec. 16 (department heads; ambassadors, public ministers and consuls; officers of the armed forces from colonel or naval captain; other officers whose appointments are vested in the President by the Constitution). Congress cannot add offices requiring confirmation by statute (a structural point that also appears in the finals coverage).

      Last-minute checklist

      • Tribunal: 3 Justices + 6 members; senior Justice chairs; ‘sole judge’ of election, returns and qualifications.
      • Jurisdiction: proclamation + oath + assumption (Reyes v. COMELEC).
      • Bondoc: no removal for party disloyalty. Abbas: all must sit. Abayon: grave abuse review.
      • CA: Senate President + 12 + 12; chair votes only to break ties; acts within 30 session days; majority of all Members.
      • Guingona: no rounding up fractions; Daza: permanent realignments; Coseteng: minority status alone gives no seat.

      Powers of Congress, its limits, delegation, and titles of bills

      Syllabus V.A.7 and V.A.8(a)(1): plenary power; substantive limits (P&S 31–37); procedural limits (ABAKADA); titles of bills; plus delegation and the publication of IRRs, which past midterms test heavily (2023 oversight committee; 2024 Bulacan IRR; 2020 finals on IRRs). 9 cases.

      Plenary legislative power

      Art. VI, Sec. 1The legislative power shall be vested in the Congress of the Philippines which shall consist of a Senate and a House of Representatives, except to the extent reserved to the people by the provision on initiative and referendum.

      The grant is broad and plenary: Congress may legislate on any matter of common interest unless the Constitution forbids it or lodges the power elsewhere (Torralba: creating municipalities). Only Congress may create legislative districts, and so provinces and cities (Sema). Congress also has plenary power over election schedules, subject to suffrage and due process (Macalintal, 2023).

      Substantive limits (Gatmaytan, P&S)

      1. Unconstitutional laws. Congress cannot pass laws beyond its power, that infringe constitutional principles, or whose purpose or effect violates the Constitution. Courts presume constitutionality and strike down only on a clear breach.
      2. Supermajority votes. Congress cannot require a higher vote to amend or repeal a law; each House passes bills by majority with a quorum. One Congress cannot bind the next.
      3. Irrepealable laws. No law can be made beyond repeal; this would deprive later legislatures of their power.
      4. Retroactive laws. Laws are generally prospective; procedural laws may apply to pending cases; ex post facto laws and bills of attainder are prohibited (Art. III, Sec. 22).
      5. The Supreme Court’s autonomy. Congress cannot exempt anyone from court fees (fiscal autonomy) or alter rules of procedure (Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)); it cannot increase the Court’s appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence (Art. VI, Sec. 30).
      6. Other express limits: the Bill of Rights; no adding qualifications to constitutional offices (SJS v. DDB); no titles of nobility (Sec. 31); no interpreting the Constitution by statute (Endencia); the money provisions (Secs. 24 to 29).
