      Gatmaytan: his book lists these five substantive limitations (unconstitutional laws, supermajority votes, irrepealable laws, laws with retroactive effect, fiscal autonomy of the Court). When a question involves a law that ‘cannot be amended except by three-fourths’ or ‘shall not be repealed’, cite this list.

      Procedural limits: the legislative veto (ABAKADA)

      After enactment, Congress may only scrutinize (budget hearings, question hour, confirmation) and investigate (inquiries in aid of legislation). It may not supervise. Any law that lets Congress, a committee, or individual members approve, disapprove, or take part in the implementation of a law violates separation of powers, and also bicameralism and presentment, because it lets Congress act with the force of law without passing a bill (ABAKADA). The same reasoning killed the pork barrel (Belgica) and the JCOC over COMELEC’s rules (Macalintal, 2003).

      Is the oversight committee valid?
      1. Does it only review, monitor, require reports, hold hearings and recommend legislation? Valid (scrutiny and investigation).
      2. Does it approve rules, budgets of an agency, or projects; deputize or direct executive agencies; or otherwise take part in enforcement? Invalid (legislative veto or execution by Congress).
      3. Save the rest of the law if separable (ABAKADA kept RA 9335 except Sec. 12).
      2023 Q3 (Tax Code Sec. 290-A, Joint Congressional Oversight Committee on Illicit Trade): reviewing BIR and BOC performance, requiring reports, holding hearings and recommending remedial legislation are valid oversight (scrutiny and investigation in aid of legislation). But the power to deputize the BIR, BOC, PNP and NBI ‘in undertaking its duties’ lets Congress direct law enforcement: execution belongs to the President (Art. VII, Sec. 17). That clause is void under ABAKADA; the rest may stand. Also: ‘in aid of legislation’ cannot cure an executive role.

      Delegation of legislative power

      Potestas delegata non delegari potest. Congress cannot delegate the power to make the law (to decide what the law shall be), but may confer discretion in its execution.

      Valid delegation (both tests)
      1. Completeness: the law sets forth the policy to be executed, leaving nothing for the delegate to decide but how to carry it out.
      2. Sufficient standard: the law fixes limits that are sufficiently determinate or determinable, to which the delegate must conform (e.g., ‘public interest’, ‘reasonable’, ‘just and equitable’ have been accepted when read with the law’s policy).
      Permitted delegations: (1) tariff powers to the President (Art. VI, Sec. 28(2)); (2) emergency powers to the President (Sec. 23(2)); (3) to the people (initiative and referendum); (4) to local governments; (5) to administrative agencies (subordinate legislation).
      • Undue delegation: People v. Vera (provincial boards deciding whether the Probation Act applies). Subdelegation by an agency to private parties is invalid (KMU: operators setting their own fares).
      • Valid: Agustin v. Edu; Zabal (proclamation as subordinate legislation under disaster laws); Garcia v. Executive Secretary (tariffs).
      Valid IRR (Gatmaytan’s book, citing Lokin)
      1. Its promulgation is authorized by the legislature;
      2. it is within the scope of the authority given;
      3. it is promulgated in accordance with the prescribed procedure; and
      4. it is reasonable (germane to the law and consistent with its standards).
      An IRR cannot amend, expand or contradict the law it implements.

      Publication and effectivity

      Laws take effect 15 days after publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation, unless the law provides otherwise (Civil Code, Art. 2 as amended by EO 200). ‘Unless otherwise provided’ refers to the date, not to dispensing with publication: all statutes, including those of local application, and all rules that implement laws must be published (Tañada v. Tuvera, 1985 and 1986). Interpretative rules, purely internal rules, and letters of instruction to subordinates need not be published. Under the Administrative Code (Book VII), agencies must also file rules with the University of the Philippines Law Center (ONAR); rules take effect 15 days after filing unless a different date is fixed.

      2024 Q3 (Bulacan Freeport Act, Sec. 29: DTI to issue IRR within 90 days, in consultation with DOF, NEDA, the Province and a representative of the airport project; effective 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation): (1) No legislative veto: Congress has no role after enactment, unlike ABAKADA. (2) Consultation with a private project representative is not a delegation of rule-making to a private party; the DTI alone promulgates, but it must not let the private developer dictate (KMU). (3) The 90-day period is directory; a late IRR is not void. (4) Publication in one newspaper of general circulation satisfies Tañada and EO 200, but the IRR must also be filed with ONAR under the Administrative Code to bind the public. (5) The law itself must supply the policy and standards (completeness and sufficient standard). Conclusion: Sec. 29 is valid.

      Title and one subject (Art. VI, Sec. 26(1))

      Art. VI, Sec. 26(1)Every bill passed by the Congress shall embrace only one subject which shall be expressed in the title thereof.

      Two purposes (Lidasan): to prevent hodgepodge or log-rolling legislation, and to inform legislators and the public of the bill’s subject so there is no surprise or fraud. Construed liberally: the title need not catalogue every provision; it is enough that it is comprehensive enough to include the general object, and that all provisions are germane to it (Giron). A misleading title voids the law, wholly if the parts are inseparable (Lidasan). A title also limits how far an enabling law can be read (Cruz v. Paras).

      2015 midterm (anti-dynasty rule in the SK Reform Act): the SK law’s title concerns the SK’s structure and eligibility; a rule on SK officials’ relatives is germane to eligibility for SK office, so it is not a rider and does not violate the one-subject rule. Since SK office is statutory, adding qualifications is valid (the ‘adding qualifications’ bar applies to offices whose qualifications the Constitution fixes). The key marked ‘valid’.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Plenary power, except as limited; only Congress creates districts (Sema).
      • Five substantive limits from P&S; plus no added qualifications; no interpreting the Constitution.
      • Post-enactment: scrutiny and investigation only; no approval or execution role (ABAKADA).
      • Delegation: completeness plus sufficient standard; five permitted delegations; no subdelegation.
      • IRR: authorized, within scope, proper procedure, reasonable; published; filed with ONAR.
      • Title rule: no hodgepodge, no surprise; liberal construction; germaneness.

      Appropriation and tax laws

      Syllabus V.A.8(a)(2): appropriation laws (Demetria to Madera) and tax laws (Tolentino to John Hay). 16 cases. Tested in 2013 (DAP-type realignment; PDAF veto), 2015 (GAA after Belgica and Araullo; tax bill origin), 2016 (confidential and intelligence funds), 2020 finals (PAO forensic lab rider).

      The provisions

      Art. VI, Secs. 24, 25(1), 25(2), 25(5), 25(7), 29(1)Section 24. All appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills, shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.
      Section 25. (1) The Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the Government as specified in the budget. The form, content, and manner of preparation of the budget shall be prescribed by law. (2) No provision or enactment shall be embraced in the general appropriations bill unless it relates specifically to some particular appropriation therein. Any such provision or enactment shall be limited in its operation to the appropriation to which it relates. … (5) No law shall be passed authorizing any transfer of appropriations; however, the President, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the heads of Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the general appropriations law for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations. … (7) If, by the end of any fiscal year, the Congress shall have failed to pass the general appropriations bill for the ensuing fiscal year, the general appropriations law for the preceding fiscal year shall be deemed re-enacted and shall remain in force and effect until the general appropriations bill is passed by the Congress.
      Section 29. (1) No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.

      Other limits: Sec. 25(3) (Congress’s own appropriations follow the same procedure), 25(4) (special appropriations must specify the purpose and be supported by funds actually available), 25(6) (discretionary funds only for public purposes, with vouchers and guidelines), 29(2) (no public money for any church or religious dignitary, with listed exceptions), 29(3) (taxes for a special purpose form a special fund), and the item veto (Sec. 27(2)).

      The pork barrel line: how doctrine changed

      1. Philconsa v. Enriquez (1994): Countrywide Development Fund upheld (legislators only recommend). Inappropriate provisions may be vetoed separately; conditions cannot be vetoed without the item.
      2. LAMP (2012): PDAF upheld on the same premise.
      3. Belgica (2013): reversal. The PDAF and similar post-enactment powers of legislators are unconstitutional (separation of powers, non-delegation, checks and balances via the item veto, accountability, local autonomy). Philconsa and LAMP abandoned on this point.
      4. Belgica (2019): lump sums are not automatically pork; valid if they meet singular correspondence or have adequate standards.
      Singular correspondence (Belgica 2013; 2019)
      1. A valid item allocates a specified amount for a specified purpose, so the President can veto it as a unit.
      2. A lump sum is valid if all its sub-uses fall under one purpose, or if it has standards fixing its use.
      3. Invalid: a lump sum for several purposes where the amounts and projects are chosen after enactment (especially by legislators).

      Transfers, savings and augmentation

      Art. VI, Sec. 25(5) requisites (Demetria; Araullo)
      1. A law (usually the GAA) authorizes the officer to augment.
      2. There are actual savings: the purpose was completed or abandoned, or efficiencies achieved, after the item was fully provided for. Unreleased or unobligated funds declared ‘savings’ mid-year are not savings.
      3. The transfer augments an existing item in the GAA (not a new project with no appropriation).
      4. The transfer stays within the officer’s own branch or office (no ‘cross-border’ transfers).
      • Demetria v. Alba (1987): a blanket authority to transfer any fund to any project is void.
      • Araullo (2014): DAP partly void (withdrawn allotments as ‘savings’; cross-border transfers; unprogrammed funds without excess revenue; projects with no appropriation). Operative fact for projects done, not for authors absent findings of good faith.
      • Pichay (2012): the President may reorganize his own office and realign its funds under the GAA.
      • Nazareth v. Villar (2013): a benefits law without an appropriation cannot be paid; savings cannot augment a non-existent item.
      • Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023): a law postponing elections to free election funds for other uses was a disguised transfer of appropriations and void.
      • Dela Cruz v. Ochoa (2018): an item for a major final output covers its integral components.
      • Madera (2020): who refunds disallowed amounts (good-faith officers do not; recipients generally do, subject to exceptions).
      • Guingona v. Carague (1991): automatic appropriations for debt service are valid; education’s ‘highest priority’ does not bar them.
      In a news question: (1) Confidential and intelligence funds (2016 midterm; the OVP controversy): they must be appropriated by law for a specific office and purpose; transferring them to another office mid-year is a transfer of appropriations; the Senate may delete or reduce them (Congress may decrease, never increase, the President’s recommendations); they remain subject to COA audit. (2) A GAA provision defunding a unit (2020 finals, PAO forensic lab): a condition that relates to the agency’s appropriation is not a rider; Congress may refuse to fund. A provision amending other laws or the agency’s structure is an inappropriate provision (Philconsa) that the President may veto. (3) A GAA provision letting DBM change agencies’ organizational structures: substantive legislation in a budget law relates to no particular appropriation and is a rider under Sec. 25(2).
      Traps: (1) Congress may reduce or delete but may not increase the President’s recommended appropriations for the operation of government (Sec. 25(1)). (2) The re-enacted budget applies automatically if no GAA passes (Sec. 25(7)). (3) The President’s item veto applies only to appropriation, revenue and tariff bills; elsewhere the veto is all-or-nothing.

      Taxation

      Art. VI, Sec. 28(1) The rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable. The Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. (2) The Congress may, by law, authorize the President to fix within specified limits, and subject to such limitations and restrictions as it may impose, tariff rates, import and export quotas, tonnage and wharfage dues, and other duties or imposts within the framework of the national development program of the Government. (3) Charitable institutions, churches and parsonages or convents appurtenant thereto, mosques, non-profit cemeteries, and all lands, buildings, and improvements, actually, directly, and exclusively used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes shall be exempt from taxation. (4) No law granting any tax exemption shall be passed without the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress.
      • Origination (Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance): the bill, not the law, must originate in the House; the Senate may propose amendments, even a substitute. The bicameral committee may add germane provisions. A presidential certification of urgency dispenses with both three separate readings and printing three days before.
      • Uniformity and equity: taxes on persons and things of the same class at the same rate; reasonable classification allowed. The progressive taxation clause is a directive, not an enforceable right (Tolentino).
      • Exemptions: only Congress grants them, by a majority of all Members, expressly (John Hay PAC: no exemption by presidential proclamation). Constitutional exemption for charitable property requires actual, direct and exclusive use; leased commercial portions are taxable (Lung Center).
      • Tariff delegation: valid within limits Congress sets (Garcia v. Executive Secretary).
      2015 midterm (income tax reform pushed by the House, opposed by the President): a revenue bill must originate in the House, which it did. The President’s objections are relevant only when the bill reaches him: he may then veto it (or particular items, since it is a revenue bill), and Congress may override by two-thirds of all members of each House.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Sec. 24 origination list; Senate may propose amendments (Tolentino).
      • Sec. 25(1) no increase; (2) no riders; (5) augmentation requisites; (7) re-enacted budget; Sec. 29(1) no payment without appropriation.
      • Pork line: Philconsa → LAMP → Belgica 2013 (reversal) → Belgica 2019 (lump sums can be valid).
      • Savings definition; cross-border transfers void (Araullo); Macalintal 2023 (disguised transfer).
      • Tax exemptions: majority of all members; express; not by proclamation (John Hay); actual, direct and exclusive use (Lung Center).

      2026 news watch

      Gatmaytan builds his questions from recent news (‘the stories may have been altered’). These are the stories from April to October 2026 that map onto your coverage, with the rule each one triggers. Each has a practice essay in the Essay trainer. Facts are as reported up to October 8, 2026; pending cases may move before the exam.

      Political dynasties: the Court orders Congress to legislate

      Kapatiran Party v. Congress (decision dated Aug. 26, 2026; released Sept. 16): Art. II, Sec. 26 is a mandatory command; 39 years of inaction is grave abuse; mandamus granted (by majority); Congress defines ‘political dynasty’; COMELEC cannot disqualify without the law. After the ruling, the Senate moved to seek an urgent certification for its bill (SB 1901, second-degree ban, pending on second reading); the House had passed HB 8389 on June 3.

      • Rules it triggers: self-executing provisions (Manila Prince; Art. II generally not enforceable); expanded judicial review of inaction; separation of powers (can the Court compel Congress?); and, for any dynasty law, whether a ban adds qualifications to constitutional offices (Sec. 26 is the constitutional source, unlike SJS v. DDB).
      • Practice: evaluate a senator’s critique; challenge to a dynasty law.

      VP Sara Duterte’s impeachment: who counts as ‘all the Members’?

      The House impeached the Vice President a second time on May 11, 2026 (257 votes). On September 23, the Senate impeachment court ruled 13–1 that ‘all the Members of the Senate’ (Art. XI, Sec. 3(6)) counts only senators legally and actually able to take part, excluding those detained, in hiding or incapacitated. On September 30, the Supreme Court dismissed three citizens’ petitions on procedural grounds (standing, prematurity). The trial pauses after October 15 for the 2027 budget.

      • Rules it triggers: verba legis and the deliberate contrast between ‘Members present’ and ‘all the Members’; quorum and coercive jurisdiction (Avelino); a detained member is still a member (Jalosjos); ripeness and standing; Francisco’s limits on the political question doctrine.
      • Practice: the two-thirds count.
      Coverage: impeachment (Art. XI) is not in your midterm syllabus. Use the story for interpretation, judicial review and quorum, not for impeachment procedure.

      Sen. dela Rosa, the ICC warrant and ‘protective custody’

      Absent since November 2025, Sen. Ronald dela Rosa appeared on May 11, 2026 (the day the ICC unsealed its warrant for the crime against humanity of murder) and voted to elect Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano as Senate President, 13–9–2. When NBI agents tried to arrest him in the Senate, the chamber placed him under ‘protective custody’; he left on May 14. Sen. Sherwin Gatchalian has been Senate President since June 17, 2026.

      • Rules it triggers: privilege from arrest (Sec. 11: not more than six years, while in session); Jalosjos and Trillanes; the Senate’s powers under Sec. 16 (officers by majority of all Members, quorum, compelling attendance, discipline), none of which includes shielding a member from law enforcement.
      • Practice: immunity and the Senate’s actions.

      Barangay and SK elections moved to 2028 (RA 12326)

      Signed September 24, 2026: the November 2, 2026 BSKE moves to November 2028, with five-year terms; Sec. 5 speaks of the ‘extension of their terms’. Atty. Macalintal’s petition (one-subject rule, legislative appointment, ‘endless extensions’) is pending; the OSG says the term of barangay officials is a political question.

      • Rules it triggers: the postponement guidelines in Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023): postponement is the exception; it needs important, substantial or compelling reasons; election fatigue and divisiveness are not enough; intervals must not be unduly long; it must be narrowly tailored. Also hold-over (tenure) versus term extension, and the title rule (Giron).
      • Practice: resolve the petition.

      The budget: unprogrammed funds and the PhilHealth ruling

      Reps. Erice and De Lima challenge the ₱150.9-billion unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 GAA; the Court heard oral arguments in April with petitions on the 2024 and 2025 budgets and asked for memoranda in July. The President’s 2027 budget (₱7.2 trillion, submitted in August) cuts unprogrammed appropriations to about ₱112 billion. In Pimentel v. House (Dec. 3, 2025), the Court voided the 2024 GAA provision that swept ₱60 billion of PhilHealth funds to the Treasury.

      • Rules it triggers: Sec. 25(1) (no congressional increase), 25(2) (riders), 25(5) (augmentation by the President only, from savings), 29(3) (special funds); Belgica 2019 (standby funds valid with standards); Araullo (excess-revenue certification); the GAA cannot amend substantive law.
      • Practice: unprogrammed appropriations; a 2027 fund sweep.

      Last-minute checklist

      • Kapatiran: duty vs content vs enforcement.
      • ‘All the Members’ vs ‘Members present’; Avelino is about quorum.
      • Arrest privilege: six years and in session; the Senate cannot grant custody.
      • Election postponements: Macalintal 2023 guidelines.
      • Budget: no increase, no riders, no transfers, special funds stay special.
